d: A shedding or pouring forth of blood (in sacrifice).

e.t: This word refers to the shedding of blood, or bloodshed. It describes the act of blood being poured out rather than the blood itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 9:22. Its basic sense is therefore specific and concrete: bloodshed or the shedding of blood. The surrounding verse determines how this act functions in that passage, but the word itself points to blood being shed.

This word means a hearer—someone who listens to what is spoken. It identifies a person by the role of listening to a message or instruction, rather than naming the message itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times: once in Romans and three times in James. Its basic sense is straightforward; the surrounding verse determines what message the hearer is hearing.

This Greek New Testament word describes someone or something as “blameless” or “unblemished”—free from fault or defect. It is used nine times across nine New Testament verses, including passages in Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, Hebrews, 1 Peter, and Revelation. Its central idea is moral or sacrificial purity: nothing blameworthy or defective is found in what it describes. One listed gloss is “spice,” but the clearer repeated sense for understanding this word is being without blame or blemish.

This word means “inexhaustible” or “not exhaustible,” describing something that does not run out or become depleted. It points to an unending supply rather than a limited store that can be used up. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 12:33. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains clear: what it describes cannot be exhausted or brought to an end.

e.t: This word means “to shake off”—to rid oneself of something by shaking it away. It describes a deliberate physical action, such as removing dust, dirt, or an unwanted object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only twice, so its basic meaning is quite focused rather than broad or abstract. The surrounding verse determines what is being shaken off, but the word itself emphasizes forcefully separating something from oneself. It can therefore describe a visible act that communicates rejection or complete removal, depending on the context.

d: A small coin equal to the tenth part of a drachma.

e.t: The word refers to an assarion, retaining the name of a specific term rather than offering a translated descriptive phrase. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, once in Matthew 10:29 and once in Luke 12:6. Those references identify where the word occurs, but the precise force of the term in either verse requires the surrounding verse and passage.

This word describes someone or something as “mute” or “silent,” without speech or an audible voice. It functions as a descriptive word rather than naming an action: it identifies a person or thing by the absence of spoken sound. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, including descriptions of a silent or mute person and references to speechless conditions. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on being unable to speak or simply being silent.

This word means “expensive” or “very expensive.” It describes something of unusually high cost or value, emphasizing that it is not ordinary or inexpensive. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. Its recorded occurrence is in Matthew 26:7, but the word’s precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The central idea remains clear: something costly, valuable, or requiring a substantial price.

This word means “slow,” describing a lack of speed or readiness. It can refer generally to something that does not happen quickly, with the surrounding sentence showing what kind of slowness is intended. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times in two verses, appearing in Luke 24:25 and twice in James 1:19. Its basic sense remains simple: being slow rather than quick in response or action.

d: To shrink, to be fearful, timid, cowardly.
me: Verb, Present, Active, iMperative, third, Singular

e.t: This word describes being timid or afraid. It points to a person’s lack of courage or confidence when facing something unsettling. In ordinary biblical use, it expresses fearfulness rather than courage or steadiness. The Greek New Testament records it only once, in John 14:27, so its broader range must be understood from this basic sense rather than from many examples.

Demetrius is a personal name, not a descriptive word for a quality or action. In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times, each time rendered as “Demetrius.” The name occurs twice in Acts 19 and once in 3 John 1:12. As with other personal names, its specific reference depends on the person identified in each passage. Its lexical meaning here is simply the name Demetrius.

me: Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, first, Singular

e.t: This Greek verb means “to put on” or “to rub on,” describing the action of applying something to a surface or person. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Revelation 3:18. The word itself expresses an act of placing or spreading something upon another thing; the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being applied and why. These meanings present the word’s ordinary sense without extending it beyond its single New Testament occurrence.

This Greek New Testament word refers to an olive garden or olive-growing place. Its meanings include “an olive garden,” “olive,” and “Olivet,” the name used for a place associated with olives. It functions as a place or tree-related term rather than describing an action or quality. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek New Testament, appearing from Matthew through Acts. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on how the surrounding sentence uses the term.

d: Bringing in (besides or in addition), introduction, importation.

e.t: This word means “introduction”: the act of bringing something in or presenting it so that access to it becomes possible. As a noun, it names an entry or approach rather than the thing being entered. In the Greek New Testament it occurs once, in Hebrews 7:19. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense points to being brought near or given access.

This Greek New Testament word means a “patch,” referring to a piece of material used to mend or cover a damaged area of clothing. It names the added piece itself rather than the whole garment or the act of repairing it. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, across three verses, in Jesus’ teaching about putting new cloth on an old garment. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: To dawn, to be near commencing.
me: Verb, Imperfect, Active, Indicative, third, Singular
Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Dative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “to dawn,” describing the beginning of daylight as morning arrives. It expresses the time when darkness gives way to the first light of day. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Matthew 28:1 and Luke 23:54. Its basic sense is an action or change in the day’s condition: the night is ending and dawn is approaching or beginning.

e.t: This word means to find, discover, or meet someone or something. It describes coming upon what was sought, recognizing what is present, or encountering a person. Depending on the sentence, it can refer to the act of finding, the result of having found something, or meeting someone. It occurs 176 times in the Greek New Testament, so its precise sense is shaped by the surrounding words and situation. Its broad use includes both ordinary discovery and personal encounter.

This word means “half dead,” describing someone who is still alive but in a severely weakened condition, close to death. It expresses an incomplete state of death rather than a person who has already died. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 10:30. The word’s focus is the person’s dangerous physical condition: life remains, but strength and well-being have been gravely diminished. Its exact force in that passage is understood more fully from the surrounding verse and context.

This word means “and,” joining words, phrases, or statements, and it can also mean “also,” “even,” or “indeed” when adding emphasis or an additional point. Its basic function is connective: it links one thought with another rather than naming an object, action, or person. It is extremely common in the Greek New Testament, occurring 9,019 times, so its precise force depends on the words and sentences it joins. These approved meanings reflect its normal range of use across the New Testament.

d: Properly: a dining couch; hence: a group of diners.

e.h: A Group Reclining for a Meal
e.t: This word refers to a group of people arranged or reclining together for a meal. It describes the group as a unit, especially in relation to how those people are gathered at the table or dining place. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 9:14. Its basic meaning is therefore specific and concrete: a meal group, rather than an individual person or the food itself.

This word means “cymbal,” referring to a percussion instrument made to produce sound when struck. It names a physical musical instrument rather than an attitude, action, or spiritual quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 13:1. Its meaning remains the name of the instrument itself; the surrounding verse determines how that instrument is used in the comparison, but the word’s basic sense is simply cymbal.

d: (Hebrew), manna, the supernatural food eaten by the Israelites in the desert: of spiritual food.

e.t: This word means “manna,” the name for the food mentioned in these New Testament passages. It functions as a noun, referring to a specific thing rather than describing an action, quality, or person. It appears four times in the Greek New Testament: twice in John, once in Hebrews, and once in Revelation. Its basic meaning remains consistent across these passages, where it is rendered “manna.” The precise significance of manna in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: A witness; an eye- or ear-witness.

e.t: This word means “witness” or “witnesses”: a person or group who bears testimony. It identifies those who can testify about what they know or have observed, and it can describe people serving publicly as witnesses. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 35 times, including passages concerning witnesses in Matthew, Mark, Acts, and Revelation. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

d: A measure, amphora, about 39.39 liters or 8.75 gallons.

e.t: This word means “measure,” referring to an amount or standard used to quantify something. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at John 2:6. The word’s basic sense identifies a measured quantity, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being measured. Its meaning is therefore simple and concrete: a measure or specified amount, rather than an action, emotion, or broader spiritual concept.

This word means “toil”—demanding, exhausting labor that requires sustained effort. It describes work viewed in terms of its hardship and weariness, rather than simply any activity or task. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in 2 Corinthians 11:27, 1 Thessalonians 2:9, and 2 Thessalonians 3:8. Its basic sense remains focused on the costly effort involved in labor. The surrounding verse determines what specific work is being discussed, but the word itself points to strenuous toil and the fatigue that accompanies it.

d: A linen cloth, a sheet, sail.

e.t: This word refers to a linen sheet or other sheet-like cloth. It names a physical object rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Acts: once in Acts 10:11 and again in Acts 11:5. Both occurrences use the same basic sense of a sheet. The word’s precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and account, but its ordinary meaning is straightforward: a sheet made of linen or a similar piece of cloth.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to sail past.” It is a verb describing movement by water as a vessel travels onward, passing along or beyond a place rather than stopping there. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in Acts 27, in accounts of Paul’s sea voyage. The word focuses on the ship’s course and progress along its route. Its precise force in either verse is understood from the surrounding voyage narrative, but its central idea remains sailing past a location.

d: Persuasion, conviction, a yielding to persuasion.

e.t: This word means “persuasion”: the influence or convincing power that moves someone toward a position or course of action. It refers to being persuaded rather than merely hearing information, though the exact force depends on the sentence and surrounding passage. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Galatians 5:8. That single occurrence presents the word as a description of influence affecting a person’s response, while its basic meaning remains persuasion or conviction.

d: Riches, wealth, abundance, materially or spiritually.

e.t: This word means “riches,” referring to material wealth or an abundance of valuable possessions. It is used as a noun in the Greek New Testament and can describe riches as something people possess or pursue. The word occurs 22 times in 21 New Testament verses, from Matthew through Revelation, showing that it is a recurring term for wealth rather than a rare or specialized expression. Its precise significance in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “foresight”: the ability to look ahead and recognize what may happen or what may be needed. It describes thoughtful anticipation rather than a reaction after events occur. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, in Acts 24:2 and Romans 13:14. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains the same: seeing ahead and making provision with that awareness.

This word refers to a fall or to falling. It describes the act or result of going down, rather than remaining upright or standing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, so its normal meaning is clear but its precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse. The word is rendered “fall” and “falling,” expressions that preserve its central idea of descent or collapse. It appears once in Matthew and once in Luke, with both occurrences belonging to this same basic sense.

This word refers to a tower: a tall, substantial structure built to rise above its surroundings. In the New Testament, it is used for a recognizable building rather than as an abstract idea. The word appears four times in the Greek New Testament, including references to a tower on a vineyard and to a tower considered when estimating the cost of construction. Its exact significance in any passage comes from the surrounding context, but its basic meaning remains a tower or elevated structure.

This word means “darkness,” describing the absence of light. In the Greek New Testament, it is used for darkness as a recognizable condition or setting, and its precise force in a passage depends on the surrounding context. It occurs 31 times in 30 verses, from Matthew through Jude. The word appears in passages concerning both ordinary darkness and language that contrasts darkness with light, so its meaning remains centered on the idea of darkness while context clarifies its use.

d: To collect an army, enlist troops.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Participle, Dative, Singular, Masculine

e.h: To Enlist or Gather an Army
e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to enlist” or “to gather an army.” It describes the act of recruiting people for military service or assembling them into an army. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Timothy 2:4. Its basic sense focuses on organizing people for military duty, while the surrounding verse determines how that image functions in its particular setting.

This Greek New Testament word means “harmony,” describing unity or accord between people or sides. It points to things fitting together rather than standing in opposition. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 6:15. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains harmony: a state of agreement and peaceful alignment.

d: A company traveling together, a caravan.

e.t: This word refers to a caravan or a company of travelers moving together. It describes a group journeying as one traveling party, rather than a solitary traveler. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 2:44, and its setting involves people traveling together. The word itself identifies the traveling group; the surrounding passage determines the specific details of that journey.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word describes acting “in self-control,” with a person’s desires and actions kept under restraint rather than allowed to rule. It expresses a manner of conduct shaped by disciplined moderation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Titus 2:12. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that sentence depends on the context, but its central meaning is conduct governed by self-control.

This word means “thistle,” referring to a prickly weed or plant. It names something that grows from the ground and is not useful as a cultivated crop. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Matthew 7:16 and Hebrews 6:8. Its basic meaning remains the plant itself; the precise force of the word in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context.

This word means “torch,” referring to a portable light used to illuminate the darkness. It names a physical object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, at John 18:3, and its ordinary meaning remains straightforward: a torch or similar flame-bearing light. The surrounding passage determines its particular role in that verse, but the word itself identifies the source of illumination being carried.

This word refers to a barrier or fence—something that blocks passage or separates one side from another. It is a noun naming a physical divider, though the surrounding sentence determines whether the barrier is being discussed literally or as a separating boundary. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, so it has a focused use rather than a broad range of meanings. Its central idea remains a structure or boundary that stands between people, places, or areas.

e.t: This word means “to dole out” or “to feed,” describing the act of supplying food to someone. It can emphasize giving nourishment directly or distributing it to another person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Romans 12:20 and 1 Corinthians 13:3. Its basic meaning remains focused on providing food, while the surrounding verse determines the specific force of that action.
